title: Ecclesiastes
speaker: Zoketsu Norman Fischer
summary: Zoketsu Norman Fischer suggests that a seemingly pessimistic biblical text like Ecclesiastes can actually be a reminder to appreciate the present moment, particularly our breath, which is both physical and spiritual. This perspective allows us to find meaning in life's impermanence and cultivate wonder and appreciation for what truly matters. By embracing this understanding, we can let go of attachments and find freedom from suffering, living more fully and authentically in the present moment.

sentences.text: *An unsurpassed, penetrating and perfect dharma is rarely met with even in a hundred thousand million kalpas.
Having it to see and listen to, to remember and accept, I vow to taste the truth of the Tathagata's words.*
Morning, everybody.

Well, today for my final talk, I'm going to switch gears altogether and perhaps oddly talk about a biblical text, which is called in Hebrew Kohelet, but mostly everybody knows it by its English name, Ecclesiastes.
Somehow I've been studying this text, and somehow the mood seems appropriate for today.
Everybody knows this text.
You know it, whether you know you know it or not.
It's very familiar, as you'll see when I quote some of it for you.
The word Kohelet is a person's name.
Ecclesiastes is a transliteration, an English version of the transliteration of a Greek word translating Kohelet, which is the name of the speaker of the text.
Probably a pseudonym, but the word Kohelet means something like the convener of the assembly.
The King James Version translates the word Kohelet as preacher, but we don't know who the person is who wrote it.
Traditionally they say that King Solomon is the author of Ecclesiastes, but now scholars are pretty sure that that's not so.
When you read it and think about it, it's actually quite an odd text, because it is the opposite of what the rest of the Bible is saying.
Its tone and its message are the opposite.

We've been talking these last several days about our human faith in goodness and our quest for truth, that we strive for goodness, and we strive for truth, and we're passionate about this striving, however much we know it's impossible.
It helps to know it's impossible.
That way we don't have to get mad at ourselves for not succeeding.
Like the four vows: beings are infinite in number, I will save them.
We already know that we can't succeed at that in any objective way.
So this idea that we're striving for the impossible, we're going forward toward better days, is something that we have deep within us, that commitment.
It's actually a deep thought in our culture.
In fact, you could say it's the theme of the Torah and therefore of the Gospels, right?
We're going forward to the promised land, or we're going to the kingdom of heaven or the kingdom of God.
Yes, it's a long journey, it's difficult, but we're going and we're going to get there someday.
That's really what the Bible and the Torah and the Gospels are saying.
But Kohelet seems to be saying the opposite.
Nothing works.
Nothing matters.
We're not on a journey going forward.
We're not going anywhere.
It just goes round and round.
We're not getting anywhere at all.
Nothing really happens.
Life is sort of a useless, pathetic exercise.
We're born, we die.
In five minutes, everybody forgets us as if we never existed.
Kohelet actually says all that.
What a downer, right?
Right in the middle of the Bible, the biggest downer of all time.
Maybe those of you who are therapists would read Kohelet and give him a diagnosis that he's maybe depressed or something like that.
But also, Kohelet can cheer you up.
When you think about Kohelet, you can think, yes, well, yeah, things go up, they go down, people are born, they die.
Things go round and round and round.
Yes, life is matter.
Life is very brief.
It doesn't matter.
But at the same time, Earth endures forever, or God endures forever.
So Kohelet is typically read at times when consolation is needed.
So here are the opening verses of Kohelet.
I know you know these verses.
This is from the King James translation.
*Vanity of vanities, says Kohelet, says the preacher.
Vanity of vanities, all is vanity.
What profit has a man of all his labor, which he labors under the sun?
One generation passes away and another generation comes, but the earth abides forever.
The sun also rises.*
That's where Hemingway got his title.
*The sun also rises and the sun goes down and hasteth to his place where he arose.*
Round and round he goes, over and over again.
The beginning and the ending and the beginning and the ending.
*The wind goes down toward the south and turns about toward the north.
It whirls about continuously and the wind returns again according to his circuits.
And all the rivers run into the sea, yet the sea is not full.
Unto the place from whence the rivers come, thither they return again.
All things are full of labor.
Man cannot utter it.
The eye is not satisfied with seeing, nor the ear filled with hearing.
The thing that hath been, it is that which shall be, and that which is done is that which shall be done.
And there is nothing new under the sun.
Is there anything whereof it may be said, See, this is new?
It already has been of old time, which was before us.
There is no remembrance of former things, neither shall there be any remembrance of things that are to come with those that shall come after.*
So that's roughly the first 11 verses of the first chapter of Kohelet, and I've been reading this and checking various translations.
I have a number of different translations, and several of them are unlike the King James Bible, which I think is a translation from the Greek.
A lot of the ones that I have are translations from the Hebrew.
I got interested in this because I heard that a brand new version has come out recently from Robert Alter, the great biblical scholar.
That's what got me thinking about this.
Here's something that I think we will all be very interested to know.
In Hebrew, the opening lines, which are translated from the Greek as vanity, vanity, all is mere vanity, the actual Hebrew word that's translated as vanity is ch'vel.
The literal meaning of the word ch'vel is mere breath.
So in the Robert Alter translation it says mere breath, mere breath, everything is a mere breath.
Zen students always sit up and take notice whenever we hear the word breath, because we're all about the breath, right?
We know what a momentous thing a breath is.
People don't think much of it, but we really are devoted to the breath.
I'm so grateful for the breath.
I think it's the greatest thing, the breath.
Where would we be without it, right?
Well, this is a little complicated, and let's see if I can explain and make it simple.

As you heard, after Kohelet says everything is a mere breath, it then goes on to talk about the sun going round and round without going anywhere, and the same with the wind blowing this way and that way without getting anywhere.
Now the word wind, actually it's the same in the Greek as the Hebrew.
In Hebrew and the Greek, the word wind and the word breath and the word spirit are the same.
So the Hebrew word that is translated here as wind means wind, but it also means breath.
It's the same Hebrew word that's used in the Bible in the opening chapters when it says in the beginning, ruach hovered over the deep in the timeless time before time.
And a little later in Genesis when it says God blows a breath into Adam, the first human, and the human comes alive.
The breath comes from God.
It's that same breath, that same wind that was there from timeless time.
So this is very mysterious, right?
Very interesting to us who've been sitting here for a whole week with nothing but the breath.
We really can appreciate what this is saying, because we've been breathing and breathing and breathing and breathing and really appreciating.
What is this breathing?
This mysterious breath that actually literally is our life and that we feel is more than just a mechanical thing.
It's not reducible to its physiology.

This breath that has been with us from the moment we were born and will be with us until the moment when we pass from this world, this breath that was here from the beginning of the beginning and before the beginning, that appears right here in us now, this endless silent breath.

So maybe we could say that the ruach, the spirit, maybe this is, I'm making this up, it's a little too simple, but we could say ruach is like the inhale, the living breath, the precious stuff of our being alive, the sacredness, the endlessness, the Buddha nature, right, of our living in every moment.
So then maybe hevel, the mere breath, means the exhale, the mere puff of air that yes brings, I hope you've experienced, calm, peace.
It brings calm and peace because it's a letting go, right?
It's a settling back into nothing.
Exhale is letting go of life, a mere breath.
So we have been discovering this breathing all week.
Breath is life, breath is love, breath is letting go, breath is peace, both living and dying, balanced and in rhythm.
And yes, where have we been getting to this week?
Nowhere really, right?
We've just been going round and round and round and round, just like it says in Kohelet.
So he's telling us we breathe in, we're active, we strive for the good, we have things to do, we have obligations and duties, and we breathe out, we relax fully, nothing to do.
We're nobody, nothing to grasp.
So maybe what Kohelet is telling us here is something deeper than the surface meaning, which sounds like, oh well, nothing matters, it's just repetitive, useless.
No, maybe he's telling us that the entire universe is breathing with us as we are living and dying, living and dying, living and dying forever.
From the point of view of our practice, this is not depressing or disappointing.
This is the beauty of awakening.
The eighth verse says, *all things are full of labor, man cannot utter it.* And in Robert Alter's translation, he translates a little differently.
He says, *all things are weary, men cannot speak of it.
The eye is not satisfied with seeing, nor the ear filled with hearing.* When I read these lines, it also made me think of our practice.

All the things we want to grab in this world, or we feel deprived of if we don't grab them, the material things, but also maybe for us who perhaps are not so concerned about material things, maybe other things we want to grab, like prestige, or some kind of personal power, or sense of accomplishment, or even just a sense of self-worth.
All these things are weary, they're weighty, so laborious, don't we know, to reach for and to carry around with us.
The world is unsatisfying.
Whatever we look at, whatever we hear, is never enough.
And I think that the Buddha taught this way.

He said, the objects of the senses will disappoint, and we will attach to them, and we will be obsessed with them because we are seeking in them more than they can provide, or we will have an aversion for them because we're attached to the peace we crave when things we don't like are removed from us.

So, in other words, our attachment and our craving, which keep us bound to suffering, come from the fact that we're looking for something through the senses, including the mind and the emotions, that we will never find in those things.

One of the great pleasures of sesshin, and I hope that in this Zoom sesshin you've also been able to feel this, as I know you do when we're in a beautiful place like Samish Island, is that you feel what it's like to just let the senses relax and come and go.
Let what you see and hear and feel and think come and go without any grabbiness.
It's just okay.
We don't need more than what comes and goes in a moment.

And then, as I read, *the thing that has been is that which will be, and that which is done is that which will be done, and there is nothing new under the sun.* It's very poetic and beautiful, but it's also, I think, a powerful statement about causality, about karma.
The past will condition the future.
There's no escape.
In the Zen stories about causality that I referred to the other day, one of the points that they make is that you don't escape, you don't get enlightened and escape the past.
The past conditions the present and the future.
The past, as you have discovered, I'm sure, never disappears.
We find that when we look at our mind, and we find that when we look at our world and we look at history, the past is alive right here.
And so what we do now, determined by the past, makes a future.
Time is momentous and intense.
Every moment counts not only because it is precious and brief, but because it never ends.
It turns and turns, including all the past and all the future, appearing and disappearing and always new.
The past never goes away, but the past is not fixed.
The past, like the present and the future, is turning round and round, and awakening is right here in this ancient and new moment.
That's why every life is so important, and every moment of every life matters so much.
More, literally more, than we can ever know.
*There is no remembrance of former things.* In other words, no remembrance of things past.
Another title for another great book, right?
*There's no remembrance of former things.
Neither shall there be any remembrance of things to come with those that shall come after.* So he's saying we're all going to be forgotten.
It's true, right?
Maybe when we die, a handful of people who knew us will remember us, but then in five minutes they'll also be dead, and nobody will remember us.
Nobody.

It reminds me of a great Thomas Hardy poem where the speakers of the poem are dead people in the graveyard, and the dead people who died not too long ago say to the people who are living, like people come alive to the graveyard, they say, you think it's bad us being dead, but this is nothing.
Because you still remember us, and you go around thinking about us, so in that way we're still alive.
But the guys in the back of the graveyard who died generations ago, that's the worst death.
They died a second time, because nobody remembers them.
No one has any idea who they are.
They're totally forgotten, and that's going to happen to us too, eventually.
So it's really bad, but it's worse than you think.
So that's right, we're all going to be completely forgotten.
And I think when you read that in Kohelet, it's like, oh geez, that's sobering.
Like, boy, I guess it is pretty meaningless to be living, we're going to be totally forgotten.
One of the deepest thoughts in the Torah is remember, don't ever forget, remember, and as you know, Jews are always remembering everything all the time.
But no, it's all going to be forgotten, you'll be forgotten.
It seems shocking, and very sobering and sad.
But then remember Dogen, right?
One of Dogen's great lines, it's the final line of a little section which begins, to study the self, to study Buddhism is to study the self, to study the self is to forget the self.
And then the last line of that little passage is, *"And this traceless awakening, traceless awakening goes on and on endlessly."* So for Dogen, leaving no trace, total forgetfulness is beautiful.
He says it's like a bird in the sky.
A bird flies through the sky, there are no tracks, there are no road signs, there's nothing that's remembered, but a bird flies in the path of its ancestors.
Even though a bird is not remembering grandfather bird who flew this way, a bird just flies that way because of the traceless awakening from the past.
So in our practice, it's a beautiful thing, this forgetting, because nothing is ever forgotten, even when it's forgotten.
So for us, it means, practically and literally speaking, that what we care about in this lifetime...
It's funny, now people my age, we're all getting really old and dying and this and that.
So one of the words that you hear people talking about is legacy.
What's their legacy?
Well, in Buddhism, nobody cares about legacy, right?
Because the point is not how important am I in this lifetime, and will all my accomplishments be remembered?
That's not for us really the point.

The point is to live, to be alive when we're alive, and to protect life and love life, and to know that as long as life goes on, as long as even being is being, or even non-being is not being, we are there.
We don't need to be remembered, because we are there in that bird flying through the traceless sky, and we've always been here.
The best mark to leave is no mark.
That's the greatest mark that we leave.
So we don't need to measure our great accomplishments or lack of them.
We need to breathe a breath, ruach and chevel, the whole universe breathing that breath with us.
And again, I'm hoping that during this week, you had one breath like that, where you had nothing to worry about, nothing to do.
Next, Kohelet talks about how he devoted his life to trying to be wise, trying to understand the truth.
And he tried through every way, through study and contemplation, but also through living, through being involved with other people.
As he describes himself in the poem, he was a powerful person.
He had wealth, he had lots of pleasures in life.
He was trying in all these ways to understand his life.
And he finds wisdom.
And here's what he says about his wisdom.
Again, what a downer, right?
He says in verse 18 of chapter 1, *"For in much wisdom is grief, and he that increases knowledge increases sorrow."* Again, a downer, right?
If you take it at face value, this is not what we were expecting.
Weren't we expecting our great wisdom to bring us peace and happiness and a good life?
But when you think about it, this really makes sense.
And it's very beautiful.
The more you come to understand about yourself and about life, the sadder it all is, really.
And you can't really fool yourself into thinking that things are going to turn out well.
No, they will not.
Best-case scenario, you grow extremely old and decrepit and maybe lose your mind, and then you die.
Fabulous.
Maturity and wisdom is maturity and suffering, right?
The longer you live, the longer you practice, it's guaranteed you will experience more and more and more suffering.
You will understand suffering better and better.
But that's not a bad thing.
That's a good thing.
Because the more suffering you experience and feel in your heart, the more love you're going to feel.
And the more poignant will be the moments of your life.
And you feel tremendous sympathy for everyone and everything that must undergo this lifetime and all that it will bring.
And you are no longer requiring of things that they be different.
And you're no longer disappointed and feeling cheated that they are not different.
In fact, the sorrow that Kohelet seems, on the surface, to be complaining about is actually quite beautiful.
So the last part I'll quote to you from Kohelet is chapter 3, the beginning of chapter 3.
And you all know this by heart, if only from the Joni Mitchell song.
Or maybe Joan Baez also recorded this and made it even more famous.
So you all know this.
*To everything there is a season and a time to every purpose under heaven.
A time to be born and a time to die.
A time to plant and a time to pluck up that which is planted.
A time to kill and a time to heal.
A time to break down and a time to build up.
A time to weep and a time to laugh.
A time to mourn and a time to dance.
A time to cast away stones and a time to gather stones together.
A time to embrace and a time to refrain from embracing.
A time to get and a time to lose, a time to keep, and a time to cast away.
A time to rend and a time to sew.
A time to keep silence and a time to speak.
A time to love and a time to hate.
A time of war and a time of peace.*
Each arising of each moment is Genjokoan, the sudden appearance of what is as awakening.
Each thing here and not here, perfect and imperfect.

Some things we like, some things we don't like, some things we support, some things we oppose, but each thing has its moment and we embrace that moment in whatever way we are able, whatever way our bodhisattva vow guides us toward, with love and acceptance, that this is what we are given.
This is the gift of this moment of our lives.
A little bit more from Kohelet:
*What profit has he that works in his labor?
I have seen the travail which God hath given to the sons of men to be exercised in it.*
In other words, life is a great labor.
It's very difficult, this life that we have been given.
*He hath made everything beautiful in his time.
Also he hath set the world in their heart so that no man can find out the work that God maketh from the beginning to the end.*

This is translated differently by Robert Alter, who says, *"He has done aptly in its time eternity to He,"* meaning God, *"has put in their heart without man grasping at all what it is God has done from beginning to end."* So this is a beautiful passage to me.
In King James it's really nice that he says, time is beauty, more or less what he's saying.
Time is beauty.
What appears in time is always beautiful because, think about it, what's the alternative?
You might not like what's going on, but think of the alternative.
Nothing.
Nothing appearing.
How beautiful that anything at all appears.
It's a miracle.
You're alive.
This appears.
But then I like what Alter says next, his translation, which I think is more exact from the Hebrew.
Of course, King James is always a little bit off because translating from one language to another to a third, there's bound to be more slippage.
So Alter is only translating from one language to another.
So he has a better chance of being more specific and accurate.
It's more or less saying here what I have been speaking about for the last couple of days.
Here it says, God, or whoever God is, or no one, or somehow the love for eternity, the love for truth beyond what we can know, is in our hearts.
The love that causes us to strive to understand what we will never understand is in our hearts.
As Nanquan says when Zhaozhou says, what is the way?
Nanquan says, everyday mind is the way.
Zhaozhou says, how can I aim for it?
Zhaozhou says, it has nothing to do with knowing or not knowing.
It's vast and wide.

As the Lotus Sutra says, and Dogen comments on this in one of his most important fascicles, only a Buddha and a Buddha can know it, which means no one can know it, but it arises between us, together in our practice, in our interaction, in our mutually being human.
We evoke it and we feel it.
Verse 12 of the third chapter:
*I know that there is no good in them but for a man to rejoice and to do good in his life, and also that every man should eat and drink and enjoy the good of all his labor.
It is the gift of God.*
And I apologize for Kohelet, of course, as all these old texts do, using the male pronoun exclusively.
He means people, not men.
We know that we can't know.
We know that we can't grasp anything, and we know we're not God.
To me, this is the great thing about God.
God is not us, and we are not God.
But God isn't not us, and we are not not God.
The whole thing is quite paradoxical.
God has no location, therefore God is every location, right here in your cushion.
It's like I used to quote when I read a book about cosmology, where they figured out this exact location in space where the Big Bang happened, in the days when they used to believe in the Big Bang.

And the mathematics showed the exact point in space where the Big Bang happened, and it was at every point in space, so that all of us, when we're sitting on our cushion in Zazen, we are sitting in the exact origin point of the physical universe.

And here, Kohelet, more or less as I read it anyway, is saying that every location and every moment of being, every Genjokoan, we could say, we could use the word God to describe each location and each happening, including, as Dogen teaches us, our delusion and our pain.
This is the paradox, the strangeness of our humanness.
And maybe our practice can help us appreciate and settle with this human paradox so that we can appreciate it and not only be okay with it, but have some love for it.

And then, as Kohelet says, we can really appreciate our life, eating and drinking, seeing and hearing the simple act of kindness, enjoying all the things that we are able to do and make, and realizing that none of this is ours, and all of it is a gift.
For me, this first ever Zoom session has been a gift.
And somehow it's very surprising how smoothly it went, thanks to everybody at Red Cedar for figuring out how to do this.
I've loved the chanting, hearing Tim chanting and chanting with Tim in the mornings and other times.
It's been great to be in Kate and Jeff's zendo, beautiful to see the lit candle and the Buddha on the altar and Kate bowing in her robes, sitting quietly in the zendo, in her seat.
And it's been a pleasure seeing all of you in your homes and bowing to you and speaking with you and seeing your faces and names on the screen like I'm seeing now.
We have been sitting in the middle of difficult times, as we've discussed.
The difficult times, no doubt, no doubt, will continue.
We shouldn't have any other expectations.
A final verse from Kohelet, the fourteenth verse of the third chapter:
*I know that whatever God does is forever.
Nothing can be added to it, nothing can be taken away from it, and it's God's doing, and we should stand in awe before it.*
So true.
Everything is forever.
Everything is just the way it is, not some other way.
This is an awesome fact, and we stand in awe before it.
I hope our sesshin has helped you feel this awe so that you can go forth from our sesshin stronger for the effort that you'll need to make as you go forward into time's beauty.
So my talk is over, but sesshin is not over.
We have a few more hours of the day to enjoy.
Please enjoy this last part of the sesshin with relaxation, but also strength and resolve.
Thank you so much for listening to my talks and for speaking with me, and I know that we will practice together more in the future.
Forever.
Thanks.
*May our intention equally extend to every being and place with the true merit of Buddha's way.
Beings are numberless.
I vow to save them.
Delusions are inexhaustible.
I vow to end them.
Dharma gates are boundless.
I vow to enter them.
Buddha's way is unsurpassable.
I vow to become it.*
*This is what should be accomplished by the one who is wise, who seeks the good, and has obtained peace.
Let one be strenuous, upright, and sincere without pride, easily contented, and joyous.
Let one not be submerged by the things of the world.
Let one not take upon oneself the burden of riches.
Let one's senses be controlled.
Let one be wise but not puffed up, and let one not desire great possessions even for one's family.
Let one do nothing that is mean or that the wise would reprove.
May all beings be happy.
May they be joyous and live in safety.
All living beings, whether weak or strong, in high or middle or low realms of existence, small or great, visible or invisible, near or far, born or to be born, may all beings be happy.
Let no one deceive another, nor despise any being in any state.
Let none by anger or hatred wish harm to another.*

*Even as a mother at the risk of her life watches over and protects her only child, so with a boundless mind should one cherish all living things, suffusing love over the entire world above, below, and all around without limit.
So let one cultivate an infinite goodwill toward the whole world.
Standing or walking, sitting or lying down, during all one's waking hours, let one practice the way with gratitude.
Not holding to* fixed views*, endowed with insight, freed from sense appetites, one who achieves the way will be freed from the duality of birth and death.*
*Respectfully, we have offered incense and chanted the Metta Sutta.
The positive energy of this assembly we offer to the great teachers who have transmitted the lamp through four countries.
May our life reveal their compassion.
May this sangha be peaceful and harmonious, stable and free from calamity, as we practice joyfully together with all beings.
All actions, three times, all bodhisattva, mahasattvas, wisdom, beyond wisdom.*
